manifest.name: @snnh/dsh-role-config
manifest.description: Role presets and a model pool for dsh: role-routed delegation with capability conditions and priority fallback

bundle.text:
# The dsh-role-config bundle patch: one row holding the role presets, the
# model pool, the routing rules, and the delegation tool wiring. The Plugins
# page edits this row's volatile fields under the id below.
#
# The row also speaks for the official delegation tool: while this plugin is
# enabled it registers a same-named `subagent` tool that routes roles. That
# shadow needs the official `tool-subagent` row to keep
# `modelSelectionSettings: false`; the plugin logs a diagnostic when the
# official tool is registered per agent instead (see README).
- insert:
    - id: role-config
      name: @snnh/dsh-role-config

readme.text:
---
description: "Role presets and a model pool for dsh: the model delegates to a role, the operator's rules pick the model, and a failure walks the role's chain."
---

English | [中文](README.zh.md)

A dsh bundle that gives delegation two ways in and one decision layer:

- **Role presets.** The model delegates to a role (`role: "premium"`) and never
  learns which model serves it. Each role carries a description the model
  reads, a priority chain, and the operator's own routing rules.
- **Model pool.** Models the model may name directly, each with the
  description the operator wrote for it. A direct route is used as given and
  never fails over.
- **Routing rules.** Before a role's chain head serves, its conditions run in
  order: prompt substrings, a regular expression, required input modalities,
  a minimum context window, or the operator's own capability tags. Nothing
  matched and AI routing is on, one bounded router call decides; if it fails,
  the chain head serves.
- **Priority failover.** A delegated child whose request fails terminally
  retries the same request on the next member of its role's chain, and the
  original failure stands once the chain is exhausted.
- **Function bindings.** Context compaction and session titles can follow a
  role instead of the session's route, or keep the harness default.

```sh
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add @snnh/dsh-role-config
```

The package is published to npm, so the line above needs no build step. A git
install (`github:snnh/dsh-role-config`) works too: the built halves
(`lib/index.js`, `lib/client.js`, and their declarations) are committed, so it
needs no build script and no `allowBuilds` permission. Rebuild them with
`npm run build` after changing `src/`.

readme.section: Nothing is on until you turn it on
readme.text:
A fresh mount registers no tool and changes no agent: `exposure.delegateTool`
and `exposure.listTool` both default to `false`, so the official delegation
tool keeps serving until an operator asks for the routed one. Turning both on
is the whole opt-in:

```yaml
- id: role-config
  config:
    exposure:
      delegateTool: true

With `exposure.delegateTool: true` this plugin registers its delegation tool under the official `subagent` name.
While the plugin is enabled that routed tool is what the agent sees; disable
the plugin and the official tool serves again. Shadowing needs the official
tool one scope further out than the agent, so the official `tool-subagent` row
must carry `modelSelectionSettings: false`:

```yaml
- id: tool-subagent
  config:
    provider: spawn
    toolName: subagent

Leave that row ENABLED. Disabling it to free the name is a one-way trade: with
this plugin switched off afterwards, the deployment has no delegation tool at
all. Nothing needs it: the routed registration is nearer than the preset scope,
so it wins the name while the official tool stays mounted and serves.
Switching the takeover off (`delegateTool: false`, or the settings page's
**Restore the official delegation tool** button, which stages that switch and
saves in one click) hands the name back, and the plugin removes a leftover
`disabled: true` from the official row while it is at it.

A profile patch reaches the rows the profile declares. The shipped presets
declare their own, nested inside a `cordis:group`, and a patch replaces a
row's whole config — so restate the preset row with that one field flipped,
the way the harness's own overlays do. `packages/bundle/web-app/presets/standard.patch.yml`
lists the shipped plugins; refresh your copy when it changes:

```yaml
- id: preset-standard
  config:
    id: standard
    order: 1

With model selection on, the official tool registers inside every agent's own
scope, where a same-named tool cannot exist. The plugin then names the row to
fix and leaves the official tool in place, so the session still opens;
`delegate.toolName` renames this plugin's tool instead, if you would rather
keep the official configuration.

Settings documents are confined to a loopback page by default, so a deployment reached at `http://<lan-ip>:<port>` shows the model pages and every plugin page as unavailable. To configure this plugin from the address you actually use, restate the `client-connection` row with its operator surface opened:

```yaml
- id: connection
  config:
    trustedHosts: !!js ctx.webRuntime.trustedHosts
    operatorSurface: trusted

A patch replaces a row's whole config, so keep `trustedHosts` in the row. The page is served only after the access token is validated and every request it makes still passes the Host/Origin fence and the session check; what changes is that the settings and plugin pages render at all.

Open **Plugins** in the Web sidebar and select **Role Config**. The page edits
one `role-config` settings section: the pool with its descriptions, the role
presets with their chains and rules, the switches (which surfaces exist,
failover, AI routing), the function bindings, and the delegation wiring.

| Surface | Content | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `list_model_roles` | Role ids with descriptions, and pool routes with descriptions | Only when the model calls it |
| System prompt | The same catalog, compact | Only with `exposure.sessionStart` |
| `subagent` (`role`) | Nothing about the chosen model | Always |

A role's members, rules, and the router's answer never reach the model.

- A role never fails over for a directly named route, and the main agent's own
  requests never fail over.
- Agent-team members inherit the lead's route; this plugin can only fail them
  over, not choose their model.
- Function bindings write the target row's configuration and have no failover
  of their own.
